questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the difference between teineigo and kenjōgo?
options: A. Teineigo elevates your own actions; kenjōgo elevates others' actions
B. Teineigo is the polite baseline (ます/です); kenjōgo uses special vocabulary to humble the speaker's own actions
C. Both teineigo and kenjōgo elevate the other person
D. Kenjōgo is only used in written Japanese, not in speech
questions.explanation: Teineigo is the ます/です polite baseline — no special vocabulary substitution. Kenjōgo uses lexical substitutions (行く→参る, もらう→いただく) to humble the speaker's own actions, showing deference to the listener.

questions.question: When speaking to a client about your boss (your uchi superior), you should use sonkeigo for your boss's actions because they outrank you.
questions.explanation: This is the uchi/soto principle. When speaking to outsiders (soto = the client), your entire in-group (uchi) — including your boss — is treated as 'down' relative to the outsider. You use kenjōgo (humble) for your boss's actions when describing them to a client: 部長は明日参ります (humble), not 部長は明日いらっしゃいます.

questions.question: A job candidate says 私が先週の面接にいらっしゃいました。What is wrong with this sentence?
options: A. Nothing is wrong — いらっしゃいました is a standard past tense form
B. いらっしゃる is sonkeigo and must never be used to describe the speaker's own actions; 参りました is correct
C. The candidate should have used 来ました instead of a keigo form
D. いらっしゃいました is too formal for a job interview context
questions.explanation: Using sonkeigo (いらっしゃる) for your own actions is the most consequential keigo error. It elevates yourself, which is socially backward. The correct kenjōgo form is 参りました (I came / I was there). This error reads as confusing or rude to a native speaker.

questions.question: Explain, in your own words, why 美化語 (bikago) is listed separately from the three main keigo tiers. Give one example of bikago in use.
questions.sample_answer: Bikago uses お or ご prefixes to make speech more elegant or refined, but does not encode a social relationship — it doesn't elevate another person or humble the speaker. It is about the speaker's own cultivated speech style. For example, saying お酒 instead of just 酒 is bikago: the speaker sounds more refined, but the prefix is not marking respect toward a specific person or humbling oneself. In contrast, sonkeigo and kenjōgo are always directional — they mark who is 'up' and who is 'down' in the interaction.
key_concepts: お/ご as elegance not hierarchy

questions.question: A department store staff member says to a customer: お待たせいたしました、田中様。Which keigo patterns are present in this sentence?
options: A. Only teineigo — いたしました is a polite past form
B. Kenjōgo (いたす as humble form of する) for the staff member's action, and 様 as an honorific for the customer
C. Sonkeigo for the customer and bikago for the store
D. This sentence contains no keigo — it is standard polite speech
questions.explanation: お待たせいたしました uses the kenjōgo pattern: お + ます-stem (待たせ) + いたしました (humble form of する). The staff member is humbling their own action (having made the customer wait). 様 is an honorific suffix that elevates the customer. Both together create the full service-Japanese register.

questions.question: In which situation is it INAPPROPRIATE to use keigo (sonkeigo or kenjōgo)?
options: A. A business call to a client company
C. A casual dinner with colleagues who have become your close friends over a year of working together
D. Speaking to a department store staff member who is helping you
questions.explanation: Overusing keigo with close colleagues creates unnecessary social distance and sounds socially awkward — as if you are treating your friends as strangers. The research notes that overusing keigo 'can create unnecessary distance or sound robotic' (Kotoba Garden Japanese). Once a close working relationship is established, teineigo or even casual speech is appropriate.
